source.author: Written for this study guide
source.grounding: help.splunk.com Splunk Enterprise 10.4, Knowledge Management Manual and Pivot Manual

questions.stem: What is the relationship between a data model and Pivot?

options.text: The data model supplies the dataset; Pivot is the SPL-free interface that consumes it to build a report.
options.explanation: Pivot cannot run without a data model. The model defines the structured dataset that Pivot then reports on.

options.text: Pivot supplies the dataset that the data model reports on.
options.explanation: The dependency runs the other way, and this reversal is a documented trap.

options.text: They are independent features that happen to share a menu.
options.explanation: Pivot has a hard dependency on a data model.

options.text: Pivot generates a data model automatically from any search.
options.explanation: Saving a Pivot-built table from a non-transforming search does create a model behind the scenes, but that is a specific flow rather than the general relationship.

questions.overallExplanation: A data model is a hierarchical, structured view of your data. Pivot is the interface that lets someone build reports from it without writing SPL. Model first, Pivot second.

guide.blueprintTitle: Describe the relationship between data models and pivot
guide.verdictNote: The printed Apress guide states this backwards, which is recorded in source-notes/apress-errata.md.

docs.title: Introduction to Pivot (Pivot Manual 10.4)
docs.note: Pivot reports are built on data model datasets.

questions.stem: How many dataset types does a data model support, and what are they?

options.text: Four: event, search, transaction and child
options.explanation: The documentation states datasets break down into four types, and child is one of them rather than a modifier of the other three.

options.text: Three: event, search and transaction
options.explanation: This omits child datasets, which the docs list as a type in their own right.

options.text: Two: root and child
options.explanation: Root is a position in the hierarchy rather than a type name, and it does not capture the event, search and transaction distinction.

options.text: Five: event, search, transaction, child and accelerated
options.explanation: Acceleration is a property you enable, not a dataset type.

questions.overallExplanation: The documented sentence is worth memorising: datasets break down into four types, event datasets, search datasets, transaction datasets and child datasets. A question offering three is the common trap.

guide.verdictNote: The transcribed practice bank keys this as three types. The fact-check corrected it against the docs, and the corrected version is what the simulator scores against.

docs.title: About data models (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: "Datasets break down into four types. These types are: Event datasets, search datasets, transaction datasets, and child datasets."

questions.stem: A data model has been accelerated and now needs a new field. What must happen first?

options.text: Turn off its acceleration; an accelerated data model cannot be edited.
options.explanation: The documentation is explicit: after you accelerate a data model you cannot edit it, and making changes requires turning acceleration off.

options.text: Nothing; accelerated models can be edited and the summary rebuilds itself.
options.explanation: Editing is blocked while acceleration is on, so no rebuild is triggered.

options.text: Clone the model, edit the clone, and delete the original.
options.explanation: This works around a restriction that has a documented remedy, and cloning is separately discouraged in the CIM guidance.

options.text: Rebuild the summary manually, then edit.
options.explanation: A manual rebuild does not unlock editing. Acceleration has to be turned off.

questions.overallExplanation: Accelerated means uneditable, not permanent. Turn acceleration off, make the change, turn it back on. The summary is then rebuilt for the model as it now stands.

guide.verdictNote: The transcribed practice bank keys this as create a new model. The docs give the turn-off-acceleration answer verbatim on the Manage data models page.

docs.title: Manage data models (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: "After you accelerate a data model, you cannot edit it. To make changes to an accelerated data model, you must turn off its acceleration."

questions.stem: Which dataset type can add auto-extracted fields?

options.text: Root datasets only; child datasets inherit them.
options.explanation: Auto-extracted fields are added at the root. Every other field type, including eval expression, lookup, regular expression and Geo IP, can be added at any level.

options.text: Any dataset, root or child.
options.explanation: This is true of the other field types but not of auto-extracted fields.

options.text: Child datasets only.
options.explanation: Children inherit rather than add auto-extracted fields.

options.text: Only transaction datasets.
options.explanation: Transaction datasets are one root type among several and have no special claim here.

questions.overallExplanation: Five field types exist: auto-extracted, eval expression, lookup, regular expression and Geo IP. Only the first is restricted to root datasets. Inheritance carries them down, and a child dataset inherits all constraints and all fields from every ancestor.

guide.verdictNote: Inheritance is cumulative, so each level down returns strictly fewer events than its parent, never more.

docs.title: Define dataset fields (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Auto-extracted fields can only be added to root datasets.

questions.stem: What does marking a data model field as Required do?

options.text: It filters out any event that does not have the field, acting as an additional constraint.
options.explanation: Required is not documentation. It shrinks the dataset, so marking a sparse field Required can quietly remove most of your events.

options.text: It marks the field as important for whoever maintains the model.
options.explanation: It has a real filtering effect rather than being advisory.

options.text: It makes Pivot require a value for the field before running a report.
options.explanation: It is not a form validation. The filtering happens on the data, not on user input.

options.text: It forces the field to be indexed at index time.
options.explanation: Data models are entirely search-time constructs.

questions.overallExplanation: Required acts as another constraint on top of the formal constraints. Compare with Hidden, which suppresses the field only for Pivot users defining a report while leaving it fully present in the dataset and reachable from SPL.

guide.verdictNote: Required and Hidden are frequently offered as each other's definition, so read the option carefully for which one filters and which one only affects the Pivot interface.

docs.title: Define dataset fields (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Required filters events lacking the field; Hidden affects the Pivot interface only.

questions.stem: Which statement about a root event dataset's constraint is correct?

options.text: It looks like the first part of a search, before any pipe or additional commands.
options.explanation: A constraint is a simple search expression. Anything needing a pipe requires a root search dataset instead.

options.text: It can include a pipe and a transforming command such as `stats count`.
options.explanation: That is what a root search dataset is for. A root event dataset constraint cannot contain a pipe.

options.text: It must include at least one search macro.
options.explanation: Macros are not required, and child dataset constraints cannot include them at all.

options.text: It is optional; a root event dataset with no constraint matches all events.
options.explanation: The constraint is what defines which events belong to the dataset.

questions.overallExplanation: Root event datasets take a simple search expression. Root search datasets take a full pipeline and are the escape hatch when you need commands, at the cost that acceleration only works if the search uses streaming commands.

guide.verdictNote: Child dataset constraints cannot include search macros, and searches referencing such datasets fail rather than degrade.

docs.title: Design data models (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Constraints look like the first part of a search, before pipes and additional commands.

questions.stem: Which data model property can never be changed after the dataset is created?

options.text: Dataset ID
options.explanation: Dataset ID accepts only alphanumerics, underscores and hyphens, cannot contain spaces, and cannot be changed once set.

options.text: Dataset Name
options.explanation: Dataset Name accepts any character except asterisks and can be edited freely.

options.text: The constraint
options.explanation: Constraints are editable, provided the model is not accelerated at the time.

options.text: The parent dataset
options.explanation: Hierarchy can be restructured while the model is editable.

questions.overallExplanation: Name is a label and is editable. ID is an identifier and is permanent, with a restricted character set. This mirrors the Name versus Label distinction in workflow actions, where one is internal and one is presentational.

guide.verdictNote: Being permanent, the Dataset ID is what SPL references, which is why `tstats` and `from` use it rather than the display name.

docs.title: Design data models (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Dataset ID cannot be changed after creation; Dataset Name can.

questions.stem: What is required before a data model can be accelerated?

options.text: The model must be shared at app level or globally, and the user needs the `accelerate_datamodel` capability.
options.explanation: Private data models cannot be accelerated, and the capability is a separate requirement on the user's role.

options.text: Nothing; any user can accelerate a model they own.
options.explanation: Both a sharing requirement and a capability requirement stand in the way.

options.text: The model must contain at least one transaction dataset.
options.explanation: Transaction datasets are not an acceleration requirement, and root search datasets built on transforming searches cannot be accelerated at all.

options.text: The underlying indexes must be summary indexes.
options.explanation: Acceleration builds its own summaries; it does not require summary indexes as input.

questions.overallExplanation: Acceleration also needs a suitable hierarchy: at least one root event hierarchy, or a root search hierarchy using only streaming commands. A root search dataset built on a transforming search cannot be accelerated.

guide.verdictNote: Ad hoc acceleration, which Pivot uses on an unaccelerated model, lives in the search head dispatch directory and is deleted when you leave the Pivot Editor.

docs.title: Accelerate data models (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Private data models cannot be accelerated; the accelerate_datamodel capability is required.

questions.stem: Which separator does `tstats` use between the data model and its root dataset?

options.text: An equals sign, as in `FROM datamodel=Web.Web`
options.explanation: tstats uses `FROM datamodel=<model>.<root_dataset>`. The `from` command is the one that uses a colon.

options.text: A colon, as in `FROM datamodel:Web.Web`
options.explanation: The colon form belongs to `from datamodel:<model>.<dataset>`.

options.text: A dot, as in `FROM datamodel.Web.Web`
options.explanation: The dot separates model from dataset, not the keyword from the model.

options.text: A space, as in `FROM datamodel Web.Web`
options.explanation: Neither command uses a bare space here.

questions.overallExplanation: tstats takes an equals sign, from takes a colon. Options that swap the two are the standard distractor pair, and both commands use a dot between the model and the dataset.

guide.verdictNote: summariesonly defaults to false, so tstats runs over accelerated and unaccelerated models alike unless you restrict it.

questions.stem: Which two statements about data model field ordering and Geo IP fields are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Fields are processed from the top of the list downward, so a field reading another calculated field must sit below it.
options.explanation: Order is functional rather than cosmetic. A field placed above its dependency evaluates against nothing.

options.text: Geo IP fields are added as Required and their types are predetermined.
options.explanation: Neither the Required flag nor the types can be changed for Geo IP output fields.

options.text: Field order in the list is purely presentational.
options.explanation: This is the belief the processing order refutes.

options.text: Geo IP fields can be marked Optional like any other calculated field.
options.explanation: They cannot. Required is fixed for them.

questions.overallExplanation: Two easily-missed mechanics. Ordering matters because fields evaluate top to bottom. Geo IP fields are constrained: fixed types, fixed Required flag, and they need an existing field of type ipv4 positioned above them.

guide.verdictNote: The ordering rule is the data model analogue of calculated fields not chaining within a props.conf stanza, though here order does help rather than being ignored.

docs.title: Define dataset fields (Knowledge Management 10.4)
docs.note: Fields are processed in descending order; Geo IP fields are Required with predetermined types.
